item.title: Discourse: Open-Source Community Forum
item.description:
Discourse is open-source community forum software. Pigsty’s app/discourse template builds the application image locally with the official classic discourse_docker Launcher and runs it with Docker Compose. PostgreSQL is managed externally by Pigsty; a single Redis instance runs inside the application container.

The template follows app.yml → application directory → .env → make. apps.discourse.dest is /data/app/discourse, keeping managed and persistent files together for migration. Use app/discourse/, conf/app/discourse.yml, and files/discourse.sql from the same Pigsty version.

item.title: Jupyter: Notebooks and Data Analysis
item.description:
JupyterLab provides interactive notebooks, terminals, and data analysis. Pigsty v4.6.0 offers two deployment options:

  • The VIBE module, managed by Ansible and systemd, for a complete Web development sandbox.
  • The lightweight standalone app/jupyter Docker Compose template documented here.

app/jupyter is not a default apps inventory entry. Prepare its data directory separately. app.yml -e app=jupyter does not handle directory ownership.

Quick Start 

cd ~/pigsty/app/jupyter
vi .env # change JUPYTER_TOKEN and optionally pin JUPYTER_IMAGE
chmod 600 .env
make dir # create /data/jupyter, owned by 1000:100
make up # docker compose up -d

Generate a strong token with openssl rand -hex 32. The default port is 8888; open http://<host_ip>:8888.

item.title: Dify: AI Workflow Platform
item.description:
Dify is an open-source platform for developing generative AI and LLM applications. It supports agent creation, AI workflows, RAG retrieval, and model management. These features help users build and operate generative AI applications.

Pigsty supports self-hosted Dify with single-command deployment. Critical state resides in externally managed PostgreSQL. You can use pgvector in the same PostgreSQL instance as the vector database to simplify deployment.

  • Quick Start
  • Why Self-Host
  • Installation
  • Configuration
  • Checklist
  • Domain and SSL
  • Upgrading
  • File Backup

The template uses Dify v1.19.0 with plugin daemon v0.6.14-local and sandbox v0.2.15. The previous v1.17.1 template was validated on 2026-10-08 for login, an existing Code workflow, and service connections on Linux amd64 with PostgreSQL 18.6. Dify v1.16 and later handle PostgreSQL 18’s built-in uuidv7() without a local migration patch.

item.title: Odoo: Self-Hosted Open Source ERP
item.description:
Odoo is open-source ERP software with CRM, sales, inventory, and other business applications. The template stays on Odoo Community 19.0 for addon compatibility and uses PostgreSQL 18.

Odoo 19 requires PostgreSQL 13 or later and Python 3.10 or later; the official Docker image provides Python.

Quick Start

On a fresh Linux x86_64 / ARM64 server running a compatible operating system:

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; cd ~/pigsty
./bootstrap # Install Ansible
./configure -c app/odoo # Generate the Odoo configuration
vi pigsty.yml # Change default passwords
./deploy.yml # Install Pigsty and PostgreSQL
./docker.yml # Install Docker Compose
./app.yml # Initialize the Odoo database and start the web container

Port 8069 is published on all host interfaces by default. Open http://<ip>:8069. The initial application login is admin / admin; change the password at first login.

item.title: Wiki.js: OSS Wiki Software
item.description:
Public Demo: http://wiki.pigsty.cc

The current Compose follows the Wiki.js 2 major-version tag (requarks/wiki:2, resolving to 2.5.317 on 2026-11-06). Stable 2.x releases are maintained in requarks/wiki-v2. Wiki.js 3.0 reached GA in November 2026 under the 3 tag; it is a major rewrite with its own requirements and upgrade procedure, so do not switch an existing 2.x deployment by changing the image tag. Record and verify the actual image version before production upgrades.

TL; DR 

cd ~/pigsty/app/wiki && docker compose up -d

Postgres Preparation 

# postgres://dbuser_wiki:DBUser.Wiki@10.10.10.10:5432/wiki
- { name: wiki, owner: dbuser_wiki, revokeconn: true , comment: wiki the api gateway database }
- { name: dbuser_wiki, password: DBUser.Wiki , pgbouncer: true , roles: [ dbrole_admin ] }
bin/pgsql-user pg-meta dbuser_wiki
bin/pgsql-db pg-meta wiki

Configuration 

services:
 wiki:
 container_name: wiki
 image: requarks/wiki:2
 environment:
 DB_TYPE: postgres
 DB_HOST: 10.10.10.10
 DB_PORT: 5432
 DB_USER: dbuser_wiki
 DB_PASS: DBUser.Wiki

 - "9002:3000"

item.title: Kong: API Gateway
item.description:
Kong is an open-source API gateway.

Pigsty’s app/kong template stores configuration in PostgreSQL. For a new empty database, explicitly run the one-time kong-migration initialization job. Normal startup does not run it automatically.

Quick Start

By default, the template binds the Admin API to the host loopback address (127.0.0.1:${KONG_ADMIN_PORT}:${KONG_ADMIN_PORT}) and publishes only the HTTP/HTTPS proxy ports externally:

cd ~/pigsty/app/kong
vi .env # check KONG_PG_* and port settings
make bootstrap # only when initializing a new empty database
make up

item.title: PGLOG: PostgreSQL Log Analysis Application
item.description:
PGLOG is a sample Pigsty application that uses pglog.sample in MetaDB as its data source. Load logs into this table, then open the related dashboard.

Pigsty provides commands to retrieve CSV logs and load them into the sample table. These shortcuts are available on the meta node by default:

catlog [node=localhost] [date=today] # Print CSV log to stdout
pglog # Load CSVLOG from stdin
pglog12 # Load PG12 format CSVLOG
pglog13 # Load PG13 format CSVLOG
pglog14 # Load PG14 format CSVLOG (=pglog)

catlog | pglog # Analyze current node's log for today
catlog node-1 '2021-07-15' | pglog # Analyze node-1's csvlog for 2021-07-15

item.title: PGWeb: Browser-based PostgreSQL Client
item.description:
PGWeb Client

PGWeb is a browser-based PostgreSQL client. Pigsty provides a small Docker Compose template under app/pgweb. By default, PGWEB_PORT=8886 in .env maps container port 8081 to host port 8886.

cd ~/pigsty/app/pgweb
vi .env # adjust PGWEB_PORT if needed (default 8886)
make up # docker compose up -d

If the portal entry resolves to the Infra node, open http://cli.pigsty. Alternatively, open http://10.10.10.10:8886 directly. The public demo is http://cli.pigsty.io.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
How mature is the MYSQL module?

This pilot module targets simple, affordable MySQL clusters. Deployment convergence, HA failover, complete three-node outage recovery, replacement at the same address, daily physical backups, and monitoring/alerts have been systematically tested. Physical backup copy-back remains manual, with a runbook. It does not aim for PGSQL-level completeness: there is no PITR, DNS/HAProxy access layer, or online topology scaling. Local Router and the NODE Layer 2 VIP are supported. Validate the module against your requirements and rehearse recovery before production use.

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
MYSQL metrics come from mysqld_exporter (mysql_ raw metrics), node_exporter backup textfiles (/var/lib/node_exporter/textfile/mysql.prom), and vmalert recording rules (mysql:ins:* / mysql:cls:*). Dashboards and alerts primarily use recording rules; this page is their complete dictionary.

files/victoria/rules/mysql.yml provides 70 module recording rules, all listed here. mysql_exporter_up = up{job="mysql"} additionally comes from Infra’s shared liveness recording rules. These recorded metrics do not appear at the raw mysqld_exporter endpoint. mysql_up is the exporter’s database connection probe result.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
MYSQL uses Pigsty’s observability stack: mysqld_exporter and node_exporter textfiles feed VictoriaMetrics, Journald/Vector send error logs to VictoriaLogs, Grafana provides 5 dashboards, and vmalert loads 70 recording rules and 8 actionable alerts.

Collection Architecture

Each MySQL node runs mysqld_exporter on 9104, collecting server and MGR metrics with the least-privilege dbuser_monitor@'127.0.0.1' account. mysql-backup also writes the local physical backup timestamp and size to /var/lib/node_exporter/textfile/mysql.prom; node_exporter reports these, and rules join them to cluster metrics by ip. item.title: Administration
item.description:
This page covers daily MYSQL operations. Declare state in the inventory and converge it with playbooks. Rerunning ./mysql.yml -l <cluster> recovers an offline member, a complete outage with all three hosts reachable, or a dead member replaced at the same IP. Physical backup copy-back and incomplete outages with fewer than three reachable hosts require the manual procedures below.

Quick Reference

Operation Command
Deploy / converge / recover a cluster ./mysql.yml -l <cluster>
Preflight without changes ./mysql.yml -l <cluster> --check
Local root client shortcut my (equivalent to sudo mysql --defaults-extra-file=/etc/mysql/pigsty/root.cnf)
AdminAPI cluster status (HA) mysh (prints dba.getCluster().status() by default)
Inspect MGR topology my -e "SELECT MEMBER_HOST,MEMBER_STATE,MEMBER_ROLE FROM performance_schema.replication_group_members;"
Trigger a backup sudo systemctl start mysql-backup (only the writable primary executes it in HA)
Remove and destroy one member ./mysql-rm.yml -l <IP> -e mysql_safeguard=false (automatically switches primary first if needed)
Stop a cluster while retaining data ./mysql-rm.yml -l <cluster> -e mysql_safeguard=false -e mysql_rm_data=false
Destroy the entire cluster ./mysql-rm.yml -l <cluster> -e mysql_safeguard=false (always retains the backup directory)

Status Checks and Shortcuts

Installation deploys /etc/profile.d/mysql.sh, which provides my for all topologies and mysh on HA nodes. Credentials are stored under /etc/mysql/pigsty/ and readable only by root. Examples use EL; on Debian/Ubuntu the MySQL service unit is mysql, not mysqld.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
What Does VAULT Do?

VAULT supplies KMS (key management) and secrets storage for a Pigsty deployment, covering three main uses:

  • Transparent data encryption: store PGSQL pg_tde master keys so leaked database disks and backups cannot be decrypted without VAULT keys.
  • Object storage encryption: store keys for MINIO (Silo) KES server-side encryption.
  • Application secrets: use KV, Transit, and AppRole to store/access passwords and API keys or call encryption services.

The first two integrations currently require manual configuration; automatic integration is still being developed. Applications can use the third immediately after deployment; see Usage.

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
This page distinguishes raw OpenBao telemetry from recording metrics evaluated by vmalert. files/victoria/rules/vault.yml defines 14 recording rules. Their results are not available from /v1/sys/metrics.

Raw metrics vary with OpenBao version, member role, and runtime state. The metrics below are those used by Vault Overview and its rules, not the full telemetry output. See OpenBao telemetry metrics for the complete list.

Label Meaning Example

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
VAULT reuses Pigsty’s observability stack. OpenBao metrics flow over HTTPS to VictoriaMetrics; service and backup logs flow through Journald / Vector to VictoriaLogs. vmalert loads 14 recording rules and six alerts, and Grafana provides the Vault Overview dashboard.

Dashboard

VAULT provides one dashboard: Vault Overview.

Vault Overview Dashboard

Vault Overview is available at /ui/d/vault-overview. Use the Cluster variable at the top to select a cluster.

item.title: Usage
item.description:
After configuring and deploying VAULT, use this page to get started. The following engines and authentication methods are enabled by default:

Path Type Purpose
secret/ KV v2 secrets engine Versioned static secrets such as passwords, API keys, and certificates
transit/ Transit secrets engine Encryption as a service; applications send data for encryption/decryption while keys remain in VAULT
auth/approle/ AppRole authentication Machine credentials for applications and automation
auth/token/ Token authentication Built-in; maximum lease adjusted to ten years

OpenBao’s API is largely compatible with HashiCorp Vault, so common Vault client libraries and tools generally work directly. See the OpenBao documentation for full usage.

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
VAULT provides eight parameters in two groups:

  • VAULT: five parameters for deployment and configuration.
  • VAULT_REMOVE: three parameters controlling cluster removal.

VAULT deliberately exposes few settings. Member count determines cluster mode, HA access reuses NODE’s VIP parameters, and other ports, directories, engines, and backup policies follow fixed conventions.

Parameter Overview

The VAULT group configures instance identity, cluster name, data directory, port, and service domain.

Parameter Type Level Description
vault_seq int I Required VAULT instance identifier
vault_cluster string C Cluster name, default vault
vault_data path C Data directory, default /data/vault
vault_port port G API port, default 8200
vault_domain string G Service domain, default vault.pigsty

The VAULT_REMOVE group controls removal safeguards, data cleanup, and package removal.

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Before deploying VAULT, define a group named vault in the inventory. There is no profile or mode parameter: the mode is derived entirely from the number of members in vault.

  • Single node: no HA; suitable for development, testing, demos, and sandboxes.
  • Three nodes: tolerates one member failure and provides HA access with an L2 VIP; suitable for production.
  • Two nodes: functional but has no fault tolerance; treat it as a single-node setup.
Members Quorum Tolerated Failures Mode Service Endpoint
1 1 0 Lab vault.pigsty points to the member
2 2 0 Warning Any member failure loses quorum
3 2 1 Production vault.pigsty points to the VIP; HAProxy forwards to the active member

VAULT uses OpenBao’s built-in Raft storage. Only one active member handles writes at a time; the remaining standby members forward requests to it.

item.title: Module: VAULT
item.description:
OpenBao is an open-source key and secrets management system (MPL-2.0), forked by the community after HashiCorp Vault adopted the BSL license and hosted by the Linux Foundation. Its API is largely compatible with Vault. Pigsty’s VAULT module deploys an OpenBao cluster in the fixed vault group as the deployment’s KMS (key management service) and secrets store. Pigsty manages TLS, auto-unseal, the HA endpoint, backups, monitoring, and lifecycle.

Current status: Beta

VAULT is in Beta. Deployment, repeated execution, rolling restarts, standby read forwarding, VIP access, and snapshot backup/recovery have been validated on a three-member Ubuntu 24.04 cluster. Grafana display, alert behavior, and other operating systems still need validation. Automatic integration is not yet implemented for PGSQL pg_tde or MINIO KES; manual configuration is required. Test thoroughly in your own environment before production use, especially snapshot recovery.

item.title: Module: MYSQL
item.description:
MySQL is a widely used open-source relational database. Pigsty’s MYSQL module installs a fixed native MySQL 8.4 LTS platform on managed nodes. Choose a standalone instance or three-node single-primary InnoDB Cluster with Group Replication. The module manages TLS, backups, monitoring, and lifecycle.

Current status: Pilot module

MYSQL is a supplementary pilot module for a simple, low-cost MySQL cluster. Its scope is smaller than PGSQL. Core capabilities have been systematically tested: deployment convergence, HA failover, recovery after a complete three-node outage, replacement at the same address, daily backups, and monitoring/alerts. Destructive procedures such as physical backup copy-back remain manual operations. See the runbooks under Administration.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
How mature is the current KAFKA module?

The v1 baseline provides dynamic KRaft, full-cluster checks, cold start and repair, serial broker admission, and dynamic controller join. It supports retirement of live or dead members and three-command failed-node replacement. It also provides strict rolling restarts, TLS/SCRAM/ACL, declared topics and users, protected credential and certificate rotation, and complete monitoring.

Production requires kafka_security: scram, an odd controller count, and sufficient brokers, RF, and minISR. You must plan capacity, reassignment, balancing, upgrades, backup, restore, and failure exercises. This module does not provide a managed Kafka service. Default plaintext suits only development or trusted isolated networks.

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
Both metric sources use job=kafka. JMX targets have a role label and collect each JVM’s internal state. Protocol targets lack role and collect logical cluster, topic, partition, and consumer-group state through Kafka protocol. Protocol exporters run on the one or two broker-capable nodes with the lowest kafka_seq. Single-broker clusters run one.

JMX is enabled by default and can be disabled per instance with kafka_jmx_exporter_enabled. See Disabling JMX for effects on metrics and discovery.

item.description:

Plan First, Then Format

kafka_seq becomes KRaft node.id. A new cluster’s bootstrap manifest freezes the random Cluster ID, initial controller identities, security profile, and initial replication policy. ABORT due to redis_safeguard enabled

This means the Redis instance you are trying to remove has the safeguard enabled. If redis_safeguard is true, redis-rm.yml always refuses to run. The switch does not check whether an instance is running.

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Concept

The Redis entity model is similar to the PostgreSQL model. It includes Cluster and Instance entities. Here, Cluster does not mean native Redis Cluster mode.

REDIS uses a single-node multi-instance deployment. PGSQL uses a 1:1 deployment. Multiple Redis instances typically share one physical or virtual node to use multiple CPU cores. Thus, the procedures to configure and administer Redis instances differ slightly from PGSQL.

In Pigsty, each Redis node belongs to one cluster. You cannot deploy instances from two different Redis clusters on the same node.

item.title: Module: REDIS
item.description:
REDIS is Pigsty’s Redis-compatible cache module. Select Redis or Valkey with redis_type. The default remains redis. Both engines support primary-replica replication, Sentinel, and native cluster mode. They share configuration paths, instance service names, monitoring, and log entry points.

redis_type: redis  # default; valkey is also supported

The role installs the selected engine and redis-exporter. Instance processes use redis-server / redis-cli or valkey-server / valkey-cli, respectively. A change to redis_type changes packages and binaries. It does not automatically validate data formats, replication topology, or rollback. Rehearse any engine change on an existing cluster. Use the same engine throughout a logical cluster.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
Which backend does the MINIO module deploy by default?

Since Pigsty v4.5, including v4.6.0, the MINIO module deploys only Silo. The sole valid minio_type is silo. MINIO is a compatibility module name and does not mean the MinIO server is running.

  • Explicitly set minio_type: silo for new clusters.
  • Both minio_type: minio and minio_type: rustfs fail during identity validation.
  • External MinIO, RustFS, or other S3 services can still serve as pgBackRest repositories. The current MINIO role does not manage them.
  • Before upgrading a MinIO cluster managed by an older release, validate the MinIO-to-Silo data compatibility, backup, and rollback procedure.

Why does the Pigsty repository still carry MinIO or RustFS packages?

Upstream MinIO switched to source-only distribution on 2025-10-15. It put the repository in maintenance mode on 2025-12-03 and archived it on 2026-04-25.

item.description:
Before deploying the MINIO module, define a Silo object-storage cluster in the config inventory. The current role requires minio_type: silo and supports these inventory deployment modes:

  • Single-Node Single-Disk: SNSD: Single-node single-disk mode, can use any directory as a data disk, for development, testing, and demo only.
  • Single-Node Multi-Disk: SNMD: Compromise mode, using multiple disks (>=2) on a single server, only when resources are extremely limited.
  • Multi-Node Single-Disk: MNSD: Multiple servers with one independent data drive each, providing compact node-level high availability.
  • Multi-Node Multi-Disk: MNMD: Multi-node multi-disk mode, standard production deployment with the best reliability, but requires multiple servers.

Use SNSD for development and testing. Three-node MNSD provides compact HA with limited resources. Use MNMD for production environments that need more capacity, throughput, and drive redundancy. SNMD handles drive failures within one server but cannot tolerate losing the server.

item.description:
MINIO is Pigsty’s compatibility module name for S3-compatible object storage. The current role deploys Silo, and minio_type accepts only silo.

Silo preserves the MinIO S3/Admin APIs, MINIO_* environment variables, disk format, and mcli client interface. It can serve as a PostgreSQL pgBackRest backup repository.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
What is etcd’s role in Pigsty?

etcd is a distributed, reliable key-value store for critical system data. Pigsty uses etcd as the DCS (Distributed Config Store) for Patroni. It stores PostgreSQL HA status.

Patroni uses etcd for cluster failure detection, automatic failover, primary-replica switchover, and cluster configuration management.

etcd is critical for PostgreSQL HA. Its own availability requires a reachable majority. Production deployments normally put three or five voting members in independent failure domains.

item.description:

Configuration Guide

INFRA primarily provides monitoring infrastructure. It is optional for PostgreSQL databases.

INFRA failures typically do not affect PostgreSQL cluster operation. Exceptions apply if you manually configure dependencies on INFRA DNS/NTP services.

One INFRA node is sufficient for most scenarios. For production HA, we recommend 2-3 INFRA nodes.

item.title: Remove
item.description:
Extension removal has two levels: drop extension objects from the database, and uninstall packages from the operating system.

Drop Extension Objects

Use DROP EXTENSION to remove extensions from the database:

-- Drop extension
DROP EXTENSION pgvector;

-- If there are dependent objects, cascade delete is required
DROP EXTENSION pgvector CASCADE;

Warning: CASCADE will drop all objects that depend on this extension (tables, functions, views, etc.). Use with caution.

item.description:

item.title: Download
item.description:
Before you install extensions, make sure that their packages are available from the local repository or an upstream repository.

Default Behavior

By default, Pigsty downloads the base PostgreSQL 18 kernel packages to the local software repository. The default extra download set is repo_extra_packages_default: [ pgsql-main ]. This set includes the PostgreSQL kernel, client, and procedural languages. It also includes basic extension packages such as pg_repack, wal2json, and pgvector.

item.title: Packages
item.description:
Pigsty uses package aliases to simplify extension installation and management.

Package Alias Mechanism

Extensions have different names at different layers:

Layer Example pgvector Example postgis
Extension Name vector postgis, postgis_topology, …
Package Alias pgvector postgis
RPM Package Name pgvector_18 postgis37_18
DEB Package Name postgresql-18-pgvector postgresql-18-postgis-3

Use a package alias to specify an extension without its RPM or DEB package name:

pg_extensions: [ pgvector, postgis, timescaledb ]  # Use package aliases

Pigsty converts each alias to the correct package names for the operating system and PostgreSQL version.

item.title: Introduction
item.description:
Pigsty includes 625 packaged PostgreSQL extensions that are ready to use.

What are Extensions

PostgreSQL extensions add database functionality without changes to the core code. An extension typically consists of three parts:

  • Control file (.control): Required, contains extension metadata
  • SQL scripts (.sql): Optional, defines functions, types, operators, and other database objects
  • Dynamic library (.so): Optional, provides high-performance functionality implemented in C

Extensions can add data types, index methods, functions, and operators to PostgreSQL. They can also add foreign data access, procedural languages, performance monitoring, security auditing, and other features.

item.title: PG Kernels
item.description:
In Pigsty, you can replace the native PostgreSQL kernel with a variant that provides specialized features.

Pigsty supports multiple PostgreSQL kernels and compatibility branches within one operational framework. These kernels provide compatibility layers, multi-master replication, graph queries, MPP warehousing, transparent encryption, and other features.

The level of Pigsty integration differs between kernels. PostgreSQL, Citus, Babelfish, IvorySQL, PolarDB, AgensGraph, and pgEdge have defined templates and configuration procedures. Cloudberry and Greenplum usually use gpsql mode. For their MPP initialization and scale-out operations, upstream tools remain the preferred method.

VIP-Manager manages the VIP. It reads the Leader Key that Patroni writes to DCS (etcd) to determine whether the local node is primary.

To enable VIP for a cluster, set pg_vip_enabled to true at cluster level. You can also enable it globally.

Pigsty includes the pgsql-migration.yml playbook for online database migration with logical replication.

The generated automation scripts can reduce application downtime to a few seconds. Logical replication requires PostgreSQL 10 or later.

item.title: Authentication / HBA
item.description:
Detailed explanation of Host-Based Authentication (HBA) in Pigsty.

Authentication supports Access Control and Default Privileges. PostgreSQL supports several authentication methods.

This page describes HBA, or Host-Based Authentication. HBA rules specify which users can access each database, from which locations, and with which authentication methods.

Client Authentication

Users must authenticate before they connect to a PostgreSQL database. By default, they use a password.

You can put the password in the connection string, but this is not secure. Alternatively, use the PGPASSWORD environment variable or a .pgpass file. For details, see psql and PostgreSQL Connection Strings.

item.title: Database
item.description:
In this context, Database refers to the logical object created using the SQL command CREATE DATABASE within a database cluster.

A PostgreSQL server can serve multiple databases at the same time. In Pigsty, define the required databases in the cluster configuration.

Pigsty customizes the default template database, template1. It creates default schemas, installs default extensions, and configures default privileges. New databases inherit these settings from template1 by default.

By default, Pigsty adds each business database to the Pgbouncer connection pool with a 1:1 mapping. pg_exporter automatically discovers all business databases and monitors their objects.

item.title: User / Role
item.description:
In this context, users refer to logical objects within a database cluster created using the SQL commands CREATE USER/ROLE.

In PostgreSQL, users belong to the database cluster, rather than a specific database. Create business users before you create business databases.

Defining Users

Pigsty defines roles and users in database clusters through two configuration parameters:

  • pg_default_roles: Defines globally unified roles and users
  • pg_users: Defines business users and roles at the database cluster level

The first parameter defines roles and users shared across the environment. The second defines business roles and users for individual clusters. Both use arrays of user definition objects.

item.title: Backup & Restore
item.description:
Pigsty uses pgBackRest for PostgreSQL backups. It supports full, differential, and incremental backups, parallel processing, encryption, and Silo/S3 object storage. By default, Pigsty configures backup and WAL archiving for every PGSQL cluster.

This chapter is the operational manual for backup configuration, management, recovery, and drills. For design concepts and tradeoffs, see Point-in-Time Recovery.

item.title: Service / Access
item.description:
Separate read and write operations, route traffic correctly, and deliver PostgreSQL cluster capabilities reliably.

A service exposes database cluster capabilities to clients. It hides the details of the underlying cluster.

Services provide stable access in production, including after automatic failover in high-availability clusters. Single-node users usually do not need services.

Single-Node Users

item.title: PostgreSQL Security
item.description:
PostgreSQL security combines authentication, authorization, network boundaries, encrypted communication, data protection, and operating procedures. Pigsty provides configuration parameters for these mechanisms. Operators must still harden, verify, and audit the deployment for its environment.

Concepts and Boundaries

Topic Content

Authentication HBA, SCRAM, certificate authentication, and credential management
Access Control Built-in roles, default privileges, database ACLs, and instance-access boundaries

Compliance Launch checks, control mappings, and evidence requirements

Configuration Reference

  • HBA Configuration: declare PostgreSQL and PgBouncer authentication rules.
  • Access Control Configuration: configure default roles, application users, object privileges, and database ACLs.
  • User Configuration: define user attributes, role membership, and connection-pool options.
  • CRIT Parameter Template: critical parameters for synchronous replication, checksums, logging, and watchdog.

Administration and Verification

  • User Management: create, update, and remove users.
  • HBA Management: refresh rules, inspect effective configuration, and troubleshoot authentication.
  • Security Considerations: production hardening and acceptance checklist.
  • Security Recommendations: minimum password, network, and file checks before installation.

The inventory describes the required state. Acceptance checks should inspect HBA, certificates, listening ports, and sensitive files on running nodes. They should also verify effective roles and privileges through PostgreSQL catalogs.

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Pigsty uses configuration to control PostgreSQL behavior. This configuration combines inventory files in ~/pigsty/conf/*.yml with PGSQL parameters. After you write the configuration, you can reproduce a customized cluster in a few minutes. The configuration includes instances, users, databases, access control, extensions, and tuning policies.

Configuration Entry

  1. Prepare Inventory: Copy a pigsty/conf/*.yml template or write an Ansible inventory. Put cluster groups (all.children.<cls>.hosts) and global variables (all.vars) in the same file.
  2. Define Parameters: Override the required PGSQL parameters in vars. The override order is global → cluster → host. The last applicable setting determines the value.
  3. Generate and Apply Inventory: ./configure -c <conf> generates pigsty.yml from the selected template. Then run ./pgsql.yml -l <cls> or bin/pgsql-add <cls> against uninitialized targets to deploy services. Use the corresponding dedicated playbooks or tags for maintenance of initialized clusters.

The PostgreSQL kernel example inventory, conf/pgsql.yml, provides a minimal example. It defines one pg-meta cluster, global pg_version: 18, and a few application users and databases. You can add more clusters to this configuration.

 # standby service will route {ip|name}:5435 to sync replica's pgbouncer (5435->6432 standby)
 - name: standby  # required, service name, the actual svc name will be prefixed with `pg_cluster`, e.g: pg-meta-standby
 port: 5435 # required, service exposed port (work as kubernetes service node port mode)
 ip: "*" # optional, service bind ip address, `*` for all ip by default
 selector: "[]" # required, service member selector, use JMESPath to filter inventory
 dest: default  # optional, destination port, default|postgres|pgbouncer|<port_number>, 'default' by default
 check: /sync  # optional, health check url path, / by default
 backup: "[? pg_role == `primary`]" # backup server selector
 maxconn: 3000 # optional, max allowed front-end connection
 balance: roundrobin  # optional, haproxy load balance algorithm (roundrobin by default, other: leastconn)
 #options: 'inter 3s fastinter 1s downinter 5s rise 3 fall 3 on-marked-down shutdown-sessions slowstart 30s maxconn 3000 maxqueue 128 weight 100'

 # define pg extensions: https://pigsty.io/docs/pgsql/ext/
 pg_libs: 'pg_stat_statements, auto_explain' # add timescaledb to shared_preload_libraries
 #pg_extensions: [] # extensions to be installed on this cluster

 # define HBA rules here: https://pigsty.io/docs/pgsql/config/hba
 pg_hba_rules:
 - {user: dbuser_view , db: all ,addr: infra ,auth: pwd ,title: 'allow grafana dashboard access cmdb from infra nodes'}

 pg_vip_enabled: true
 pg_vip_address: 10.10.10.2/24

 pg_crontab: # make a full backup 1 am everyday
 - '00 01 * * * /pg/bin/pg-backup full'

 #----------------------------------#
 # pgsql cluster: pg-test (3 nodes) #
 #----------------------------------#
 # pg-test ---> 10.10.10.3 ---> 10.10.10.1{1,2,3}
 pg-test: # define the new 3-node cluster pg-test
 hosts:
 10.10.10.11: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary }  # primary instance, leader of cluster
 10.10.10.12: { pg_seq: 2, pg_role: replica }  # replica instance, follower of leader
 10.10.10.13: { pg_seq: 3, pg_role: replica, pg_offline_query: true } # replica with offline access
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-test  # define pgsql cluster name
 pg_users: [{ name: test , password: test , pgbouncer: true , roles: [ dbrole_admin ] }]
 pg_databases: [{ name: test }] # create a database and user named 'test'
 node_tune: tiny
 pg_conf: tiny.yml
 pg_vip_enabled: true
 pg_vip_address: 10.10.10.3/24
 pg_crontab: # make a full backup on monday 1am, and an incremental backup during weekdays
 - '00 01 * * 1 /pg/bin/pg-backup full'
 - '00 01 * * 2,3,4,5,6,7 /pg/bin/pg-backup'

 # redis ms, sentinel, native cluster
 #----------------------------------#
 redis-ms: # redis classic primary & replica
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { redis_node: 1 , redis_instances: { 6379: { }, 6380: { replica_of: '10.10.10.10 6379' } } } }
 vars: { redis_cluster: redis-ms ,redis_password: 'redis.ms' ,redis_max_memory: 64MB }

 redis-meta: # redis sentinel x 3
 hosts: { 10.10.10.11: { redis_node: 1 , redis_instances: { 26379: { } ,26380: { } ,26381: { } } } }
 vars:
 redis_cluster: redis-meta

 redis_sentinel_monitor: # primary list for redis sentinel, use cls as name, primary ip:port
 - { name: redis-ms, host: 10.10.10.10, port: 6379 ,password: redis.ms, quorum: 2 }

 hosts:

item.title: Module: PGSQL
item.description:
PGSQL is the core Pigsty module. An Ansible inventory declares PostgreSQL clusters. Patroni and etcd manage high availability. pgBackRest provides backup and PITR. HAProxy, VIP, DNS, PgBouncer, and the observability stack expose and monitor database services.

This page follows the Pigsty v4.6.0 source layout. For exact defaults, use the parameter reference. Keeping defaults in one reference prevents conflicting or outdated copies.

Modeling and Configuration

  • Cluster model: clusters, instances, identity, and roles.
  • Architecture: relationships among Patroni, etcd, service access, and observability.
  • Cluster configuration: primary, replica, offline instance, synchronous commit, standby cluster, delayed cluster, and Citus.
  • Kernel: PostgreSQL major version, distribution, and package selection.
  • Users, databases, HBA, and ACL: business objects and access control.
  • Service access: read-write/read-only services, HAProxy, VIP, DNS, and pooling.
  • Extension catalog: the 625 currently packaged extensions and their platform coverage.

Deployment and Administration

Task Entry point
Initialize a cluster or add an instance Cluster administration · pgsql.yml
Create or change users User administration · pgsql-user.yml
Create or change databases Database administration · pgsql-db.yml
Change HBA or parameters HBA administration · Component administration
Patroni switchovers, maintenance, and incidents Patroni administration
Install, create, update, or remove extensions Extension administration
Monitor an external instance pgsql-monitor.yml
Prepare a migration Migration · pgsql-migration.yml
Remove an instance or cluster Safe removal workflow · pgsql-rm.yml

pgsql.yml, pgsql-user.yml, pgsql-db.yml, and related playbooks change the target environment when run. By default, pgsql-rm.yml can delete data and backups. First identify the exact cluster or node and verify a recent backup. For removal, the operator must also type and confirm the exact target.

item.title: Immich: Self-Hosted Photo and Video Library
item.description:
Immich is a high-performance, self-hosted photo and video management application. It is a popular open-source alternative to Google Photos, licensed under AGPL-3.0. Features include web and mobile uploads, album sharing, timelines, maps, EXIF and RAW support, and LivePhoto. It also provides semantic search, facial recognition, and automatic backups.

The template follows Immich v3 and uses VectorChord by default for similar-image search, smart search, and face-search vectors. On 2026-10-08, both Server and ML images resolved to 3.3.0. item.title: Maybe: Self-Hosted Personal Finance
item.description:

Pigsty’s app/maybe template connects stateless Maybe Web / Worker containers to Pigsty-managed PostgreSQL. Local Redis provides the Sidekiq queue. Financial data resides in a PostgreSQL cluster with backup, monitoring, and recovery support, rather than an ephemeral Docker volume.

item.title: Configuration Templates
item.description:
Use -c with configure to select a template; the default is meta. configure accepts bare names (such as full) and searches in this order: conf/ → ha/ → fork/ → app/ → demo/ → build/. All subdirectories are under conf/. The first matching file wins. An explicit path such as ha/full selects only that template. Leading ./, the conf/ prefix, and the .yml suffix are optional.

For example, -c full and -c ha/full select conf/ha/full.yml; -c pgsql and -c fork/pgsql select conf/fork/pgsql.yml. Use halo / fork/halo for OpenHalo and mysql / demo/mysql for the native MySQL 8.4 example.

item.title: Hermes: AI Agent
item.description:
app/hermes provides a source installation guide for Hermes Agent. It uses a separate Python virtual environment and external model APIs on an existing Pigsty Linux host. The directory contains no Compose file or conf/app/hermes.yml; app.yml is not required.

The installation guide pins v2026.9.24 (Python package version 0.21.5) and requires Python >=3.11,<3.14.

Installation

Install system dependencies such as python3.12-venv, then run on the target Linux host:

set -euo pipefail
curl -fL -o /tmp/hermes-agent.tar.gz \
 https://codeload.github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/tar.gz/f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f
printf '%s %s\n' \
 babbdb9706ad1c96708d75914afb45d809cd4b73dec1ceae233a6814f5ed97e3 \
 /tmp/hermes-agent.tar.gz | sha256sum -c -

HERMES_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.hermes/hermes-agent-v2026.9.24"
test ! -e "$HERMES_INSTALL_DIR"
mkdir -p "$HERMES_INSTALL_DIR"
tar -xzf /tmp/hermes-agent.tar.gz -C "$HERMES_INSTALL_DIR" --strip-components=1
cd "$HERMES_INSTALL_DIR"
python3.12 -m venv venv
./venv/bin/python -m pip install --upgrade pip
./venv/bin/python -m pip install -e '.[pty,mcp,cron]'
./venv/bin/python -m pip check
./venv/bin/hermes --version

This release uses an editable source installation. The CLI is included in the core dependencies; the old cli extra is no longer used.

item.description:

item.description:
Pigsty can deploy Supabase on your physical, virtual, or cloud servers with a single command. Self-hosting provides more extensions, performance options, control, and potential cost savings.

As of August 2026, the official Supabase self-hosting guide recommends Docker and classifies other implementations as community projects. Pigsty is an independent community integration and is not currently listed on that page.

This tutorial requires basic Linux knowledge. Otherwise, consider using Supabase cloud or plain Docker Compose self-hosting.

item.title: Applications
item.description:
Pigsty applications have two categories:

  • Software Templates: Deployment resources under ~/pigsty/app/<name>, mainly using Docker Compose. Hermes provides a separate source installation guide.
  • Data Applets: PostgreSQL + Grafana analytics demos, mainly for learning and showcase use.

Use app.yml, app/<name>/, and conf/ from the same release to keep templates and initialization scripts compatible.

Application Model

The recommended application deployment workflow is:

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; cd ~/pigsty
./bootstrap
./configure -c <template> # e.g. app/dify, app/immich, app/jumpserver, app/maybe, supabase
vi pigsty.yml # edit passwords, domains, IPs, and secrets
./deploy.yml # deploy infrastructure and databases
./docker.yml # install Docker
./app.yml # launch applications

app.yml copies the app/<name> template to /opt/<name> (or apps.<name>.dest), prepares directories from apps.<name>.file, writes a .env file with mode 0600 from apps.<name>.conf, then runs the application’s default make target. Use apps.<name>.args to select other Make targets. Application startup inherits proxy_env proxy variables; --check mode skips the actual make execution.

item.title: PostgreSQL Mongo Mode
item.description:
The mongo template (conf/fork/mongo.yml, selected with -c mongo or -c fork/mongo) is a PostgreSQL deployment mode, not a standalone Pigsty module. It consists of:

  • PostgreSQL 18 managed by the standard PGSQL module
  • The documentdb extension and its required preload libraries
  • A stateless FerretDB proxy deployed with Pigsty’s Docker APP workflow

PostgreSQL manages all data, high availability, backups, monitoring, and the database lifecycle. FerretDB provides only the MongoDB wire-compatible endpoint.

Quick Start

The default template is a single-node deployment on 10.10.10.10. FerretDB listens on loopback by default.

The mssql template (conf/fork/mssql.yml, selected with -c mssql or -c fork/mssql) replaces native PostgreSQL with Babelfish, which provides the Microsoft SQL Server wire protocol (TDS) and T-SQL compatibility. The repository provides packages compatible with PG17 and PG18; the template defaults to pg_version: 17. See the package list for platform availability.

configure accepts both -c mssql and -c fork/mssql; both preserve the template’s PG17 settings and ignore -v. To use PG18, update both the cluster and global pg_version values in the generated inventory and verify that the kernel packages and extensions are available for your platform.

item.title: pg19
item.description:
pg19 is the single-node PostgreSQL 19 Beta evaluation template. It follows the meta topology and enables the beta repository. The local repository’s additional cache contains only core PGSQL packages. The template does not preinstall extensions.

  • Node Count: Single node
  • PostgreSQL Version: 19 Beta
  • Use Cases: New-version evaluation and compatibility testing

item.description:
The infra template deploys the Pigsty monitoring infrastructure, including VictoriaMetrics, Grafana, VictoriaLogs, and Nginx. It does not deploy PostgreSQL or etcd.

Use it as a standalone monitoring system for external PostgreSQL or RDS instances and other data sources.
